So, I originally intended to call this subreddit GamingHistory (on Reddit), but that was taken. Didn't bother disputing it, even though if you go there it's only a single post. The content of that post though is a good discussion starter, so I would like to put this here so we don't have to deal with it later.

Everyone's probably gone to their search engine of choice and looked for "First video game", once you realized even Pong had ancestors. Since I am doing a comprehensive history, I looked into all the available candidates I could find, which were most of the usual ones.

You can look at all of the pre-Tennis for Two games that I intend to talk about in detail on my database, which isn't many. There's a very large history of Chess playing devices going all the way back to 1912 that I don't intend to discuss in detail, but go check out Alex Smith's post on it. His own musings on the other candidates is also good for getting you acquainted with the usual discussion.

Of course, the biggest thing here is defining the term of video game. Personally, I am not so hung up on the semantics of the "video" portion as much as the "game" part. Let me post an excerpt from my video series script which deals with the Cathode Ray Tube Amusement Device.

It's from this point that a debate about the Cathode Ray Tube Amusement Device's credentials as a video game come into question. It was not digital, nor did it emit video signals, despite the fact that it used the same technology as a TV set. However, something to keep in mind as we move forward is that early video games had a wide array of possible display technologies (some of them not even on a screen) and signaling out one type of display as that of a “true” video game would mean excluding a great deal of important pieces in this history. That, and the term “video game” would only emerge once the mainstream took hold of it.

These are most of the periphery elements which make up the criticism of including the Cathode Ray Tube Amusement Device in any given history. Alex smith certainly doesn't, and I do not myself define it as a video game either. I include it for reasons of completionism and to, hopefully, describe the debate to others without going too far into semantics.

The next few entries on the database talk about the nature of display systems. NIMROD used lightbulbs, Berite the Brain appears to have used incandescent lights held inside televisions, but Draughts may have been displayed on a CRT.

The Mark 1 [computer] had cathode ray tube display capability, and in fact was the only output for the machine until the Manchester computer installed paper tape as a new read-out. Whether it was laboriously punched out or set onto a screen, like this modern recreation, Strachey succeeded in creating the first multi-platform, programmable video game.

To me, the method of read-out is irrelevant, and I would count Stratchey's program as being the first true "video game". People like Ralph Baer, however, are very strict in their definitions of what constitutes a video game. As some have noted, under Baer's definition we are no longer playing video games in the literal sense, because CRT televisions must be involved.

To anyone who has looked into this, or perhaps just browsing through, give me your thoughts.

What was the first video game, as far as you're concerned?

I believe it's Christopher Strachey's Draught's program, created in 1951.

What is your definition of a video game, and what are the flaws in that definition?

It must be transistor-run programmed, stored or no, which functions via interaction in a game-like manner. This allows inclusions of games which do not have a direct display, and in turn opens up the gates for many systems which are perhaps not "games" in their own right.

What is the Cathode Ray Tube Amusement Device?

A product which we can't examine beyond its patents. Whether it could have ever qualified as a video game is based on an assumption that it at one time functioned, which we cannot verify.

In the wake of Konami's unknown financial situation, I wanted to talk a bit about the drama which surrounds companies in times of hardship. For journalists and historians alike there is a desire to emphasize the drama of situations in order to tell a more compelling story, especially when there is a rebound. Perhaps that's why the Wii-U keeps being touted as a complete and utter failure, but that's a topic for another time.

Two "well known" stories of near-bankruptcy that I would like to examine come from two Japanese companies: Nintendo and Squaresoft. Well, specifically with the former it was Nintendo of America.

I'm sure that most have heard the story of how Donkey Kong was built from the hardware of another Nintendo arcade game called Radarscope, specifically to appeal to the American market. I have no idea how the business semantics of this project worked out, and we're likely to never fully know. This is what Steven Kent's Ultimate History of Video Games says.

Radarscope did not appeal to American audiences, and Judy and Stone were unable to sell all 3,000 units. Since Nintendo of America covered their expenses, they did not incur debts, but they also received very little income since they were being paid a straight commission (156).

What this implies is that Nintendo were not the ones hurting, but rather specifically Al Stone and Ron Judy, which would have left them unable to be profitable partners. This is what the Gamasutra article says on the matter.

Alas, Radar Scope was not a hit in America. In fact, it sold only 1,000 units, leaving 2,000 arcade machines with very expensive hardware sitting in Nintendo's warehouse. The implications were potentially devastating. Nintendo could either give up, and face financial ruin, or it could develop a conversion kit that would turn those cabinets into something marketable. Arakawa begged his father-in-law to pursue the latter course of action (1).

So now Arakawa is "begging" to keep Nintendo of America afloat. Granted, this article is more about the programming firm behind Donkey Kong and Radarscope, but represents something we cannot verify (unless anyone can read that Japanese book they cite). This next description comes from a news site.

After the relative failure of an arcade game called Radar Scope, Nintendo assigned a young developer named Shigeru Miyamoto to design a new game. In what is considered one of the earliest “platform” games (where a player controls a character across various platforms) and one of the earliest games with a story, Donkey Kong was developed

So a "relative failure". That may be more moderate, but is it more accurate simply by that virtue? Replay by Tristan Donovan is more vague.

...The Japanese designer's debut game was commissioned to pull Nintendo's US operation out of a hole. Nintendo of America had bet everything on Radar Scope, a Space Invaders-style shoot 'em up that had been a hit in Japanese arcades, but only sold 1,000 of the 2,000 machines it built for the US market (100).

Note how he also lowered the figure from 3,000 machines to 2,000. I checked his sources page and he doesn't seem to be citing anything in particular for that figure, unless it's buried somewhere in sales data.

Let's move onto a perhaps more pervasive tale. Lately I've been looking into Final Fantasy because I intend to interview the original programmer, Nasir Gebelli, about his life and work at Squaresoft. In most retellings of the making of the original Final Fantasy though, there's almost always the claim that Squaresoft were going out of business and that Final Fantasy saved them. This is from a thorough paper dealing with rising Japanese game companies in the mid to late 80s.

Consumers gradually became aware of the trick and the market started to slow down in 1986. In the following year, Square made a critical decision. It relocated to a shabby office in Ueno, the old downtown area of Tokyo, and also laid off half of its staff. It concentrated the efforts of the remaining 30 employees and its limited capital on a ‘final fantasy’. If not successful, the company would have to close down (12).

I was actually surprised to re-read and find that Kent is not actually the originator of this telling. His sole focus is on Sakaguchi's desire to leave.

In an effort to get more excited about his work, Sakaguchi decided to switch genres and work on a game that would be more interesting to write. He decided to create an RPG and bring the idea to his boss...

Since he planned to quit making games after this first RPG, Sakaguchi named his game Final Fantasy (540).

I believe Power-Up by Chris Kohler also states the same, but I don't have a copy on hand. Other sources point to Squaresoft being reluctant to make it for fear of it not selling, which seems a bit counter to the idea that they were betting the house on this game. From a 1-UP interview,

Mr. Sakaguchi had wanted to make an RPG long before that, but he couldn't get permission from the company, because the company said, "Well, we're not sure that will sell." But with Dragon Quest proving that a game like that could be successful, we were finally able to get that going. It all started with that.

Here's also a translation of an interview from Famitsu magazine that explains the whole development more thoroughly. Again, no mention of Squaresoft going under. An interview from Develop Online states it more clearly.

The series name, Final Fantasy, is often attributed to Square’s dependence on the product as its last throw of the dice – but the truth, says Sakaguchi, was that it was his personal last effort.

So, what to make of this? The first source I linked doesn't provide any actual numbers, which would be rather definitive if that were the case. None of the interviews seem to express any fear or time crunch during the development of the product, nor anything about a "shabby" working building. There's a lot of contradiction here, though most of the sources seem to tend towards Sakaguchi's version of events.

These are just some things to be looking out for when dealing with history. We are dealing not only with people, but with storytellers, and while it may be easy to see when someone is conflating their role when you can see an actual interview, reading is far more ambiguous. These tales of financial troubles are undoubtedly present in the industry, but how truly widespread were these beliefs, and did it always come on the cusp of great success or normal relapse?

King's Quest is an example of this narrative explored with no falsehoods involved, just straight facts of a desperate struggle for sustainability. It's hardly a neat story, with several months of absolute flux and nothing happening, but it's still compelling. This is what I want to get across when telling these histories. Semantics don't have to be boring, and one shouldn't conflate statements without asking for direct confirmation.

Now I turn the table over to you.

Do you believe that Nintendo of America was facing the possibility of being shut down prior to Donkey Kong's success?

Was Squaresoft nearing bankruptcy before they released Final Fantasy?

Do you think framing historical events as a "comeback" benefits the reader or the author more?

If the PS4 and Xbox One use common APUs that are made of an x86 processor and standard graphics core, why aren't emulators out already?
They are to new so hipsters don't care.

The reason for the lack of emulators for these consoles is the same reason that emulators for the original Xbox have exceptionally low compatibility rates. Even though the devices use the same architectures as standard computers, the exact setups still have differences that would have to be accounted for. In each case, the hardware has a very specific structure that developers have to account for in their game development. I don't know the exact reasons why Xbox emulation is so far behind PS2 or GC emulation, but I know that it has to do with the fact that the x86 architecture is fairly complex in the way it runs.

It's pretty much this, along with Nividia adding a bunch of custom shit that isn't documented to the XBox, which causes a whole lot of problems with emulation. The good documentation of the Gamecube (because of the Dolphin project) was what led to such early and good Wii emulation.

The other main reason is that most people really don't about XBox emulation: most of the popular games are on other systems, either GC/PS2 or PC. When emulation is 95%, it tends to get abandoned until someone really passionate comes along (see ZSNES being used extensively until bsnes was built because of a single guys passion).

Well, first of all, Jaguar is AMD64, not standard x86.

Secondly, they're proprietary APUs. The public doesn't know exactly what AMD's got going on in the GPU portion, so they're operating on blind reverse engineering as always.

Lastly, these are ridiculously powerful compared to their predecessors, which were vastly more powerful than their predecessors. Consider that plenty of machines still struggle with emulating PS2 hardware.

So I've been talking about this database, which you can find by clicking on this sentence.

Let me explain what this is about. A long while ago, I got very fed up with the inability to find good sources on video game history. They exist, most certainly, but are generally poorly maintained o don't cite their sources clearly enough to trust. I am very much a skeptical researcher, and though I'm not an absolute stickler for first hand accounts, I want to be able to read as close to the original as possible.

I am currently working on a script for a video series which will cover from the beginning of electronic entertainment up until 2013 (that is, ending after 2012). There are a lot of focuses for this project, but in terms of what games make the cut, it's focused on how game design trends have evolved over the years.

The second big focus is to allow people access to the information discussed in these videos so that they can make their own conclusions. Thus, the database. Every source that I reference regarding a game will be cited according to the database. This is similar to a structure seen on Ken Polsson's site, though I didn't actually remember seeing this until I already started my citation.

Let me give you an example of how you can browse this database by providing an unedited sample from my script. This is a section on MUD, or "Multi-User Dungeon".

VO: [(G) 40, G1] The capabilities of text-based games really could help it break barriers in many other powerful ways, and the thing which had helped proliferate the mainframe game culture would be central to its next definitive evolution. [(P) 85, P2(9)] In the United Kingdom at Essex University, an enterprising programmer named Roy Trubshaw started getting himself engrossed in interactive fiction. He was the secretary of the Essex Computing Society, and they experienced the one-two punch of Adventure as well as the unfinished version of Zork called Dungeon which had leaked out of MIT. [(P) 85, P1(2)/P5(1)] Captivated by it and eager to program, he started working out his own interactive world of sorts in Fall of '78, calling upon friend Richard Bartle to help him actually form it into a game. Just as with Zork, this game was to be built by the community, [(P) 85, P3(1)] but Trubshaw did this in a more literal sense. [(G) 85, G1] The game was to be multiplayer, both so that they could be the first, and to tackle a challenge yet unseen. They intended for the game to askew the normal conventions of the text adventure, bringing it closer to an RPG experience, though a few simple puzzles were present. Trubshaw stored the parser and actual world objects in a file which could be added to during the actual game, but this would prove to become large and subject to erroneous additions, so he scrapped the entire project as written in late 1979 [(S) 85, L1(291-292)/S1/S2].

First thing is the "VO" and all that stands for is "voice-over" as opposed to "OS" where I will be "on-screen". Second, we have a small reference in brackets. It refers to "G", so the first thing to know is that you're looking for a game. Go to the fortieth entry (in this case it's under tab "41" because of the headings) and yo will see that the game "Adventure" is what's currently being show on screen. Go over to column "V" and you will be able to find the source of the gameplay that I use in the video itself.

Next we have "P" which stands for "Picture". Go back to the row for MUD and head over to pictures. Click on the second link. Because there's another number in parenthesis, that means there's a particular picture on this page that I'm showing, because there are multiple. The 9th picture should be the one which is being shown on screen around that moment. Same with the following one, with the slash inferring multiple pictures.

At the very end there's an "S" indicated sources. These are the sources which are relevant to the information discussed in that paragraph, as they sometimes overlap. The first one is "L" which stands for "Literary Source". Go to the first Literary Source and if you have a copy of Replay by Tristan Donovan, you can corroborate the information in this paragraph on those pages. If a source has parenthesis after it, that likely means that there are several pages, and the page indicated will have the information relevant in that chunk.

Finally let's mention the bits of the database which serve as a guiding hand rather than specific referencing. First comes the name, obviously, though I try to list what the absolute original name was, including Japanese pronunciation an less common names than we know of them today like "Spartan-X" being the name for the classic "Kung-fu". Following that are the authors. If they are on equal ground, like Bartle and Trubshaw, they exist in the same space. If one has more of a technical role than the specific "designers", they are put into parenthesis. Publishers are always secondary, only put there if there's no "second partner" on the team.

The approximate release date comes next. This whole project is absolutely rigid when it comes to chronology. It's one of the main points I wanted to make, since I had no idea how interconnected/detached a lot of events in this history were. I think it will be insightful, though I've had people tell me "You should be telling narrative strings". Nope, everybody's already done that. Next in line is the platform the game was originally released on. If it in and of itself is a platform, or the bit is not actually a game, then it's left blank.

The penultimate row are personal notes telling myself what I should remember to mention, along with a date confirmation as I found it. In this case, Trubshaw specifically said that the "full" version of MUD was released on Easter of 1980, so that's my guiding date. Finally there's the "genre" section, a very contentious one. We can talk about why I name my genres the way I do, but in this case I have a split. I believe that MUD is more of an RPG and just uses text input, but I haven't had the opportunity to play it of yet (it is available online).

So that's a quick walkthrough of my database. If you have questions about the games included, not included, particular sections of my script, or anything else feel free to ask. I would like to posit the following questions though.

Was this database easy to navigate for you?

Is the ordering of information disorganized?

How do you judge the credulity of sources? Peer review? Talk on forums? Contacting the author?
My Database and How to Use It
